Steinhoff, House of Cards

By: Mart-Marie Faure | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Beleaguered Steinhoff's web of complex accounting shenanigans came to light recently when the company revealed their situation as fragile and in desperate need of a short term solution.

Unique Selling Point:
We ask Dr Christo WIese if and how Markus Jooste deceived him and the entire Steinhoff Board board comprising of accountants.
How could he not have seen this happening?
Steinhoff latest note to shareholders reflects a company heading towards liquidation. In a presentation to bankers in London recently, Steinhoff admitted that there are several very valuable businesses within the group but that the current position is fragile and the need for a solution in the short term is critical. The list of shareholders suing the company is starting to look as if they believe the company will be broken up or liquidated. Steinhoff is being sued by ex-chairman Christo Wiese for R59 billion and by prominent banker GT Ferreira for R1.5 billion. Tekkie Town has filed for a reversal of the Steinhoff acquisition claiming the sale was done on fraudulent terms. We will speak to experts trying to find answers on how it was possible for Markus Jooste to construct the scheme that saw the company plunge intoa scandal. Who was in on it? Whas Steinhoff's board deceived or party to the House of Cards.


Summary:
On the 6th of December 2017, Steinhoff International CEO Markus Jooste announced his resignation amid the retail giants admission of irregularities in its financial accounts. The Steinhoff share price plummeted wiping R121 billion from its market capitalization. It wiped billions off the net worth of tycoons such as Christo Wiese and GT Ferreira, and of the pension funds of millions of ordinary South Africans.
Jooste had built a house of cards. He would allegedly lend money to a company domiciled in Europe but never disclosed that the European company was run by a related party close to Jooste. Steinhoff would then charge interest on that loan, which would recognize in the income statement as revenue. For all intents and purposes, it was a fictitious debtor: that main debt would never be repaid and that debt would be classified as "cash and cash equivalents in Steinhoffs books. this resulted in operating cash flow not matching the profit it reports in its books.
The bottom line: Steinhoff's revenue was artificially inflated, and so were the assets.

Press Release:


For years, analysts, banks and ratings agencies promoted global retailer Steinhoff as a sound investment. With 40 brands under its belt and operating in over 30 territories, the retail giant was one of the top performers on world markets, that is, until the House of Cards came tumbling down. Billionaire businessman and former chairman of the company Christo Wiese is suing Steinhoff for R59 billion, but was he really unaware of the accounting fraud and financial irregularities happening right under his nose? Carte Blanche puts Wiese in the hot seat.

Script:


Steinhoff

V/O For years, global retailer, Steinhoff was one of South Africa’s investment darlings. With 40 brands under its belt and operating in 30 countries, investing in the company seemed a clear winner. But in December 2017 Steinhoff's auditors refused to sign off on the audited financials as a result of suspected accounting fraud, by hiding bad debts and inflating company value. CEO Markus Jooste resigned, shares plummeted with 300 billion rand in share value lost. It all came tumbling down like a house of cards.

Devi Link The Steinhoff debacle lifted the lid on shady goings on in corporate South Africa …… but who needs to be held accountable? The Board, the former CEO Markus Jooste, fund managers ….. or the auditors

V/O But who wouldn’t buy into the Steinhoff success story. After all billionaire businessman Christo Wiese was at the helm as chairman of the board . There were 4 Chartered accountants in the executive and off course business whizzkid CEO Markus Jooste.

Pieter Retief

Pensioner

Steinhoff was a good company, it was profit making and it was liquid.

V/O Based on Steinhoff’s market credentials , Piet Retief bought shares in the company to invest for retirement.

Pieter Retief

Pensioner

I never thought that anything could go wrong with Steinhoff, with such a wonderful chairman and his best Afrikaner directors I never thought anything could go wrong.

V/O When the bubble burst, now Ex-Chairman Wiese, claimed that the news came as a total shock. He told a parliamentary committee that it was a total bolt from the blue and that he never

suspected anything. But Global Fund Manager Zwelake Mnguni says that’s hard to believe. Wiese wasn’t just any old director. He was a highly paid non-executive chairman who appeared to have close links with the company.

Zwelake Mnguni

Chief Investment Officer

Benguela Global Fund

Managers M36 There's no way he could say he didn't know. M30 .The board has a responsibility to hold the executive accountable.. I think the challenge we have now is that the board became to cosy with the executive.

V/O So who better to ask if he knew or didn’t know or even suspected anything than Christo Wiese himself.

Christo Wiese M12 Why on earth would somebody if he's aware of things that are rotten, why would he put the money that he's worked for for 53 years, 59 billion rand, why would he put it.. to achieve what? I mean I could put my money anywhere. Why would I choose to put it in what I know is a rotten barrel of apples. Why would anybody do it, unless you're insane.

Devi M8 So there were no warning signs, nothing... Not a sausage. No funny business... Nothing that made you call MJ up and say listen I'm a little bit worried...

Christo Wiese Nothing, absolutely nothing.

Devi M9 Do you feel silly now? Well, yes and no, You know the difficulty is, Devi and I've said this before, there is no way in the world that one can build large businesses if you do not trust people.

Nobody ever suggested anything in Steinhoff that would be pushing the envelope, legally, regulatory, whatever.

V/O Again, Mnguni disagrees - he personally raised concerns about irregularities as early as February 2017 stating that the matter has been floating around since 2015.

Zwelake M18 I wrote to Christo Wiese Chairman of the board at the time. It took him 3 months to respond. And his response was I prefer that we meet in person and discuss their issues (M20).Then we arranged a flight to Cape Town to go meet with him and we were told he's not able to meet with us.

Christo Wiese Devi: This is a letter Well aware of it. They must put their point, they must come to the shareholders meeting, the general meeting of shareholders, because you must remember it's not one person's view that counts, there's a body of shareholders.

V/O

One of the big questions remaining on the minds of shareholders, regulators and government officials is whether the Board acted negligently? Should they all be held liable?

James-Brent Styan This company was at the time, 1 December 2017 sitting at a market capitalisation, so that’s the value of the company broadly of R240 billion. … today it’s sitting at about 13 billion. So, that’s roughly what? About 220 billion in value lost, double what the Gupta's allegedly took from this country.

V/O James-Brent Steyn is the author of Steinhoff, Inside South Africa’s Biggest Corporate Crash.

James-Brent Styan 00: 00:04 The Government Employee Pension Fund

lost 20 billion. Those are teachers, nurses, policemen and politicians, which is probably why parliaments had two hearings already.

Devi Link The brunt will be felt by ordinary South Africans who trusted that their monthly pension contributions and investments were in safe hands

V/O So, how could this happen? After all, Markus Jooste was the man with the midas touch. What could go wrong?

Christo Wiese M4 I looked at the liquidity of the Steinhoff shares and thought that's a good deal. M5 and obviously strongly influenced by the fact that here was this man running this big corporation Steinhoff.

DEVI

M4 So explain to me how did everybody drop the ball?

Christo Wiese

It's difficult and not so difficult. Fraud – and everybody who's in business will tell you that – is an extremely difficult thing to detect in a business that operates in 30 countries, employ hundreds of thousands of people. But it becomes almost impossible when the people at the top, your top management, if they are committing fraud it becomes virtually..... It becomes virtually impossible.

V/O Since his resignation in December 2017 Markus Jooste has not been available for comment on any of the allegations of wrong doing.

James-Brent Styan This company was a darling. It really was. And, you know, if you look at the numbers, you look at how the share price was growing and that’s, I suppose, was the cardinal sin. The people were just happy to… to stick around while this company’s numbers were so good and they were signed off by reputable people.

V/O But like Zwelake Mnguni, James believes that the warning signs were there but ignored.

James-Brent Many of the warning… warning signs that I’ve

highlighted and highlight in the book I asked them, what about these warning signs, what the heck was happening here? Hmm. [00:16:57] And they told me, you know what, those were the first items on the agenda of our board meetings.

Devi

Christo Wiese M3 So even when there were all those rumours that Steinhoff was paying too little tax, that issue of the corporate tax, that the company was inflating earnings and obscuring the losses, all of that the investigations were done, you said it was devoid of any truth? It was devoid of any truth in terms of all the information that the board got from very highly paid forensic investigators.

V/O But, many believe that a broken corporate governance structure was at the core of the disaster and by ignoring the warning signs the executive failed to protect shareholders?

Christo Wiese M11 Who was the biggest shareholder, Devi? Would I be inclined to protect myself? I think when you've worked as hard to put things together as I have, you certainly leave no stone unturned to protect your interest. If you protect your shareholding then per definition you protect the shareholding of the other shareholders.

V/O So, is Christo Wiese just another victim?

Zwelake

M41 I definitely don't think he's a victim. I think he may not have been actively involved in the fraud, but I think his desire, his self-interest is what led to this disaster, All he focussed on was externalising his assets. So he's not a victim,

Devi

M14 I'm not being insensitive when I say to you with great respect, Dr Wiese, I find it difficult to feel sorry for you because you still have a couple of billion left.

Christo Wiese I don't blame you for saying that and let me immediately assure you. The last thing I want is for people to feel sorry for me. It's in a way demeaning.

Devi

Christo Wiese

M31 What would you like to say to South African who are watching this programme. Are you sorry for whatever happened? Clearly I am sorry that I was in effect dragged into something that has done huge harm to a reputation that I spent my life building, that it has hurt people, not only financially - I'm sorry and I'm sorry for the damage that is done.

V/O But is saying sorry enough for those who have lost their pensions and life savings.

Piet Retief

Pensioner In total I lost quite a few million from Steinhoff which is really a lot of money, hard earned money that my wife and I worked for in our various businesses throughout the 50 years of being an entrepreneur.

For all intents and purposes, it was a fictitious debtor: that main debt would never be repaid and that debt would be classified as "cash and cash equivalents in Steinhoffs books. this resulted in operating cash flow not matching the profit it reports in its books. The bottom line: Steinhoff's revenue was artificially inflated, and so were the assets.
